title: Hagar in the Wilderness
lead: God sees the person everyone else has abandoned.
questions: Who around you is reduced to their status, and when did you last speak to that person by name?
In what situation has despair narrowed your field of vision, and what kind of eyes should you ask for today?
Who do you refuse compassion because they helped bring on their own misery, and how is that like Hagar’s story?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A woman, a foreigner, a slave. Three reasons not to notice her. In Abram’s household Hagar is taken, given, sent away, and no one ever once speaks to her by name. Sarai calls her only “my maidservant.” When, after being humiliated, she flees into the desert, the real story begins: “The angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert.” Found her: which means He was looking.

This is the first appearance of the Angel of the LORD in the whole Bible. The figure Scripture will recognize as God Himself makes His entrance not in the patriarch’s tent, but by a desert spring, next to a pregnant runaway slave. The first word He speaks is her name: “Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?” In this whole story, God is the first to call her by name. The Lord had asked a similar question of Adam, who dodged it, and then of Cain, who lied. Hagar answers simply: “I am running away from my mistress.” God can work with any truth. What He cannot work with is our not being honest with Him.

Hagar receives the first annunciation in the Bible: “You have conceived and will bear a son. And you shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.” She is not promised that her suffering will end. She is given the certainty that she has been heard. And then she does something no patriarch or prophet ever dared: she gives God a name. The only name given to the Creator by a human being in all of Scripture is “the God who sees me.” It was given by a woman whom no one in her own household saw.

Years later Hagar is driven out into the desert with her child. When the water runs out, she sits down “about a bowshot away”: too far to help, too close not to see. God hears the boy crying “where he lies,” under a bush, at the end of the world. “Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.” He didn’t create a well. He opened her eyes. The well had been there all along. Despair narrows our field of vision, and rescue is often within reach before we are able to see it.

The same sequence, with a voice from heaven and rescue within sight, will soon be repeated with Abraham on Mount Moriah. God doesn’t have two scripts, a better one for the chosen and a worse one for everyone else. He has one: hear, call by name, open the eyes, save.

The last two readings were about people of the promise: Abraham, who went out into the unknown, and Sarah, who lived to see her son. Today’s reading is about someone who had no share in that promise at all. A woman, a foreigner, a slave. That’s three reasons not to notice her. Every ancient society would have agreed to pass her over. The Bible does the opposite: it is in her story that things happen for the first time which later become the experience of the greatest.

sections.heading: She Took and Gave
paragraphs: It starts with an idea that was legal and sensible in that world. After ten years of waiting, Sarai offers her husband her Egyptian maidservant: “Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her.” The laws of the day knew this arrangement well. Not directly, but unmistakably, the narrator objects. He does it through his choice of words: Sarai “took” Hagar and “gave” her to her husband, and Abram “listened to the voice of Sarai.” These are exactly the same verbs, in the same order, that described the scene with the fruit in Eden. The woman took and gave; the man listened. A Hebrew reader heard it immediately: in that family, the events of paradise had just been replayed. The biggest problem, and not only in this story, is putting our own solution into action instead of trusting God’s promise.

There is something in this scene that hurts even more than the idea itself. Hagar appears in it only as an object. She is taken, given, sent. Neither Abram nor Sarai speaks to her even once. Sarai calls her “my maidservant”; years later, as Sarah, she will say “the slave woman.” In the house where she lived for years, no one spoke of her by name.

There is one more word in the text that shows whose side the narrator is on. The way Sarai treated Hagar is described with a verb that means to oppress, and it is exactly the same word the book of Exodus will later use for Israel’s fate in Egypt. A Hebrew woman oppresses an Egyptian woman before the Egyptians begin to oppress the Hebrews. The narrator doesn’t judge Sarai directly; he does it through his choice of words. And God, as we will see, hears the cry of the oppressed no matter which side it comes from.

sections.heading: He Found Her
paragraphs: Humiliated by her mistress, Hagar flees into the desert, toward Egypt, toward home. A pregnant woman, alone on a caravan route. And here comes the sentence where the real story begins: “The angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert.” If He found her, He was looking.

This scene is the first appearance of the Angel of the LORD in the whole Bible. The figure who speaks here with God’s authority and is at times identified with Him enters the pages of Scripture not in the patriarch’s tent, not at an altar, but by a desert spring, next to a pregnant runaway slave. Above all, He speaks to her by name: “Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?” In this whole story, God is the first to address her by name.

Notice, too, when Hagar finally speaks. The Bible does not record a single word of hers in all the years she lived in Abram’s household. She speaks for the first time in the desert, alone, in conversation with God. There are people who never get a word in where they live, and only the Lord God can open their hearts.

The question itself has a pedigree. Adam heard “Where are you?” in the garden. Cain heard “Where is your brother?” God asks about things He already knows, because His questions aren’t for gathering information but for opening a conversation. But there is a difference: Adam dodged, and Cain lied. Hagar answers with one simple sentence: “I am running away from my mistress Sarai.” The Egyptian servant is more honest than the first human beings. God can work with any truth, even the hardest. What He cannot work with is a relationship with Him that lacks honesty.

sections.heading: The God Who Sees Me
paragraphs: Then something happens that will never be repeated anywhere else in Scripture. Hagar hears an announcement: “Behold, you have conceived and will bear a son. And you shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.” This is the first annunciation in the Bible, the first time a child is named before birth. The kind of scene that will later take place in Nazareth appears in the Bible for the first time not with a princess or a prophetess, but with a slave woman at a desert well. And the name of the child to be born means “God hears.”

Notice what Hagar does not receive. She is not promised that her suffering will end. The angel sends her back to the house where she was humiliated. Instead she receives something else: the certainty that her affliction has been heard and that her child has a future. Sometimes that is the form in which hope comes first: not as a change of circumstances, but as the certainty that someone sees.

And then Hagar does something unique in all of Scripture: she gives God a name. “So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: ‘You are the God who sees me,’ for she said, ‘Here I have seen the One who sees me!’” It is an extraordinary moment. A woman whom no one in her own household saw calls God the One who sees her. We should remember that in Scripture “God saw” often means more than just looking. When we read that the Lord sees, it means He cares and acts. Just as “remembered” in the story of Noah, so “sees” in the story of Hagar: with God these are verbs of movement.

The well where all this happened was given a name: Beer-lahai-roi, the Well of the Living One who sees me. And it doesn’t disappear from the story. A few chapters later the text notes that Isaac, the son of the promise, settled by this very well. The heir of the great story makes his home at a place named by a slave woman. Scripture doesn’t treat her experience as a marginal episode; it turns it into a place to live.

sections.heading: About a Bowshot Away
paragraphs: Some fifteen years later the story repeats itself, only more dramatically. After Isaac is weaned, Sarah demands, “Expel the slave woman and her son!” Abraham gets up early in the morning, puts bread and a skin of water on Hagar’s shoulders, and sends her away into the desert with the boy. This time there is nowhere to run. This isn’t flight; it’s exile.

The water runs out. Hagar leaves her son under a bush, walks off, and sits down “about a bowshot away,” saying, “I cannot bear to watch the boy die!” A bowshot is too far to help and too close not to see. She couldn’t bring herself to go any farther. She sits facing him and weeps aloud.

And the text says something surprising: “God heard the voice of the boy.” Not her crying, though she was the one weeping aloud. The angel calls from heaven: “Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies.” Where he lies: right there, where he is, under a bush, at the end of the world. God didn’t wait for someone to carry the child to a better place. He heard him where he lay. The name Ishmael, “God hears,” has just stopped being theory.

The angel begins with the words “Do not be afraid.” In Genesis, God speaks these words to three people: Abram, Hagar, and Isaac. A runaway slave receives exactly the same message as two patriarchs. There is no second-class version. And it’s worth remembering that neither Hagar nor her son is blameless in this story: she once looked down on her mistress, and he mocked Isaac. God isn’t rescuing innocent victims here, because there are none in this family. He rescues the afflicted, even when they have helped bring on their own affliction. If God’s help were only for people with a clean record, no one would ever receive it.

And here is the sentence at the heart of this scene: “Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.” The text doesn’t say the Lord created a well. It says He opened her eyes. The well had been there all along. Despair has a way of narrowing our field of vision down to the size of our misfortune. Rescue is often within sight long before we are able to see it. Sometimes the whole prayer we can manage is a request for eyes.

sections.heading: A Rehearsal for Moriah
paragraphs: This scene has a twin in the Bible. The chapter about Ishmael’s expulsion and the chapter about the offering of Isaac are built from the same elements. In both, Abraham gets up early in the morning and places a burden on someone’s shoulders; in both, the road leads into the wilderness, a child is a step away from death, an angel calls from heaven, and rescue is within arm’s reach from the start. Once it is a well, once a ram in the thicket. In the entire Hebrew Bible, God’s messenger calls from heaven only in these two stories: to Hagar in the desert and to Abraham on Mount Moriah.

This pairing says something important about the God of this book. The experience that, in the very next chapter, will befall the father of faith in the most famous scene of the Old Testament was lived through, in its entirety, by an Egyptian slave woman first. God doesn’t have two scripts, a better one for the chosen and a worse one for everyone else. He has one: hear, call by name, open the eyes, save the child.

The last lines of this story close it with a tenderness that is easy to miss: the boy grew up, settled in the wilderness, “and became a great archer.” The child whose death his mother couldn’t bear to watch from a bowshot away grows into a man who makes his living with a bow. The measure of the mother’s despair became the son’s trade. God has a sense of humor.

And at the very end we see one more thing. In chapter twenty-five we find Ishmael’s genealogy: twelve sons, a dry list of names. Every promise made to Hagar is checked off in it. God kept His word even to the son who was not the child of the promise. If He did not forget the promises made to those who were passed over, how much more surely will He keep the ones confirmed by an oath.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: In Hagar’s story everything happens the other way around. The first annunciation in the Bible goes to a slave woman. The Angel of the LORD comes for the first time to a foreigner. The only name a human being ever gave to God comes from a woman everyone overlooked. As if already in the sixteenth chapter of the first book God wanted to say: remember whom I see first. In our church communities, too, there are people who live the way Hagar lived in Abram’s house: everyone talks about them, no one talks to them. Described by their status, not by their name. This story says that God is already with them, at their well. The question is whether we will follow Him there.
